abstracts.abstract: This paper presents a novel theoretical framework reconceptualizing human-computer interaction as a distributed cognitive ecosystem rather than a unidirectional user-system dialogue. Current HCI theory predominantly frames interaction through information processing metaphors that inadequately capture the emergence of meaning in complex interactive systems. Drawing upon enactivist philosophy and ecological psychology, we introduce the Interaction Affordance Dynamics (IAD) model, which posits that user cognition, interface properties, and environmental contexts co-constitute interaction outcomes through reciprocal coupling mechanisms. The framework operationalizes three constructs: perceptual anchoring, action scaffolding, and semantic resonance, which together explain how users dynamically calibrate their mental models during sustained engagement with interactive technologies. We validate the theoretical contributions through a systematic analysis of 127 empirical studies spanning two decades of HCI research, demonstrating that phenomena previously attributed to usability deficits are more parsimoniously explained through the lens of interaction dynamics. The IAD model offers HCI theory a paradigm shift from deterministic design prescriptions toward acknowledging the emergent, context-sensitive nature of user experience. This contribution extends cognitive ergonomics by providing a generative framework for predicting interaction breakdowns and designing resilient systems that accommodate human variability.

The Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and its extensions have dominated user modeling research for three decades, yet increasingly reveal limitations in predicting acceptance of emerging interactive systems characterized by high complexity and uncertain utility. This paper advances user modeling theory by integrating constructivist epistemology with TAM, proposing the Cognitive-Appraisal TAM (CA-TAM), which incorporates mediated perception, situated cognition, and affective valuation as moderating factors in technology adoption. Unlike prior extensions that primarily add constructs without addressing TAM's foundational assumptions about user rationality, CA-TAM fundamentally recontextualizes perceived usefulness and ease of use within the user's experiential horizon. We conducted a meta-analysis of 94 empirical studies (N=28,450) to establish structural equation models comparing predictive validity across technology categories. Results demonstrate that CA-TAM explains 23% more variance in behavioral intention (ΔR²=0.23, p<.001) for emerging technologies including artificial intelligence assistants, augmented reality interfaces, and ambient computing systems. The improved model maintains backward compatibility with TAM while providing enhanced explanatory power for human-computer interaction scenarios where traditional constructs prove insufficient. This contribution refines HCI theory by offering practitioners a validated instrument for predicting user adoption with greater accuracy in contemporary interactive systems.

This paper introduces Metamorphic Interfaces, a novel interactive paradigm enabling user interfaces to fundamentally transform their interaction design vocabulary based on real-time cognitive load assessment. Existing adaptive systems modify interface properties within predefined design spaces, yet remain constrained by assumptions encoded during development. Our approach transcends this limitation through a generative design architecture that constructs novel interaction modalities on-demand, utilizing a deep reinforcement learning framework trained on extensive human factors data to synthesize interface configurations never explicitly designed. The Metamorphic system continuously monitors cognitive ergonomics indicators including gaze patterns, microexpression analysis, physiological stress markers, and interaction latency distributions through multimodal sensing. When cognitive overload is detected, the system generates alternative interface representations that preserve semantic continuity while fundamentally altering presentation paradigms. We implemented the system for complex data analysis workflows and conducted a longitudinal evaluation (N=48 participants, 8 weeks) comparing Metamorphic Interfaces against conventional adaptive interfaces and static designs. Results demonstrate 47% reduction in task completion time (p<.001) and 62% improvement in user-reported experience scores for high-complexity tasks. This contribution establishes human-centered computing principles for generative interface synthesis, representing a paradigm shift from designing-for-adaptivity toward designing-for-emergence in interactive systems.

Collaborative interfaces for distributed teams remain plagued by awareness failures that undermine computer-supported cooperative work effectiveness. This paper presents Collaborative Sentinel, an enhanced interaction design that significantly improves upon existing awareness mechanisms through multimodal cue integration and predictive context modeling. Prior approaches to shared workspace awareness have relied predominantly on visual indicators that introduce information overload and require active monitoring. Collaborative Sentinel addresses these usability limitations by implementing a peripheralized awareness system that surfaces contextually relevant teammate activities through ambient displays, haptic notifications, and semantic audio cues calibrated to individual attention states. The system incorporates a machine learning model trained on collaborative interaction patterns to predict information needs and proactively deliver awareness cues before explicit requests occur. We conducted a controlled evaluation comparing Collaborative Sentinel against established CSCW tools using a collaborative design task paradigm (N=72 participants in 36 dyads). Results indicate 38% reduction in coordination breakdowns (p<.001), 29% improvement in task synchronization efficiency, and significantly enhanced user experience scores for distributed collaboration scenarios. The system demonstrates particular efficacy for asynchronous collaboration windows, addressing a persistent challenge in human-computer interaction for distributed teams. This contribution advances interactive systems design by providing a validated approach to peripheral awareness that maintains focus while ensuring necessary coordination information reaches collaborators.
